name: Rafael Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential. What is a normal shift like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 43 and a junior operator on a powder-coating conveyor for metal railings. I finished secondary school and still need the lead to check my spray-gun settings. I hang sections, watch the oven and inspect corners under a lamp. The smooth finish is satisfying; cleaning a clogged nozzle after a stopped run is not.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at home, and do you use AI?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner handles appointment calls at a dental clinic. We have two school-age children and a mortgage, with about three weeks of expenses saved. I earn a lower operator rate, Saturday shifts disappear when orders slow, and there are few similar factories nearby. I use AI every day for fault-code explanations, but verify against the machine manual and the actual gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the powder-coating shift a small AI gain might tidy the repair log, but it won't tell whether a railing came through with a bare corner. I still have to inspect the metal under the lamp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I get the junior rate, and we have only three weeks of expenses behind us. The plant has been cancelling a Saturday shift whenever rail orders slip, and there are few similar jobs nearby. A mild AI outcome leaves that ordinary wage risk in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep hanging rail sections on the coating conveyor and checking coverage with the lead. I already use AI every day to explain fault codes, then confirm them in the machine manual. I'll record the actual cancelled hours so my partner and I can plan the mortgage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the missing Saturdays, even though I am interested in the small software help. The bills don't wait for a full order book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the AI fault answer fail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month the coating gun clogged, and the AI explanation named a pressure sensor. The lead found powder packed in the nozzle, so I cleaned it only after we isolated the gun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do shifts affect your family week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner handles appointments at a dental clinic, and our two children are at school. We use a paper calendar for shifts and school collections because an extra Saturday changes who can take them.

The **Saturday rota** matters more to our mortgage than a tidier log.
think: Three weeks of **savings** cannot cover many cancelled coating shifts.
Few nearby **factory openings** make replacing junior pay difficult.
do: **Keep** hanging and inspecting coated railing sections with the lead.
**Record** cancelled Saturdays against the mortgage and childcare calendar.
feel: **Anxious** about existing lost hours despite modest AI change.
S0.quote: The bills don't wait for a full order book.
fieldNote: He already uses **AI daily** for fault explanations and verifies the actual machine before touching it.
The **thin reserve** and cancelled Saturdays justify anxiety in the mild case.

steps.text: Keep hanging railings and checking powder-coat coverage
Record cancelled Saturdays before making household spending decisions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AI may book clinic appointments and plan coating orders before robots handle the railings. The union should ask both employers for real paid training and proper notice of cut hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner's clinic appointment work could shrink soon, and our weekend shifts are already patchy. With three weeks saved, that is a risk to our mortgage, not a distant technology story. I'm keen to learn the new coating controls if the plant gives us access and a safe paid trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask our shift representative to take the cancelled-hour log into the union meeting. If the plant offers a paid supervised session on the new AI oven-control screen, I'll learn to adjust the temperature alarms on an idle batch and compare its readings with our hand gauge. My partner will ask the clinic for a written hours plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious because two wages could shrink at once. My partner's clinic appointment work could shrink soon, and our weekend shifts are already patchy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe oven-screen trial involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the supervisor the AI oven screen needs a test on scrap rail pieces, not a customer's gate. The trial must be offered and supervised before I use the new controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your partner ask the clinic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner would ask which appointment calls move to software and whether the clinic will reduce paid desk hours. We can then put the actual number next to our mortgage and food costs.

think: My partner's **desk hours** and my own Saturdays could both shrink.
I would learn **new AI controls** in a paid safe session if offered.
do: **Bring** cancelled-hour evidence to the union shift meeting.
**Learn** AI oven alarms if a paid supervised place is offered.
**Ask** the clinic for a written desk-hours plan.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic two-wage household loss.
S1.quote: My partner's clinic appointment work could shrink soon, and our weekend shifts are already patchy.
fieldNote: The **new learning** is an AI oven-control screen, beyond his existing daily fault-code queries.

steps.text: Bring cancelled coating hours to union shift meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 might take the clinic calls, and capable robots around 2031 could hang, coat and inspect rails. I'd say the union needs income protection while people learn the new machines, not a poster telling them to be flexible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the clinic to cut much of my partner's paid desk time, and later robots could take the basic hanging tasks that earn my junior wage. Three weeks of savings will not bridge either loss. I have lain awake adding up mortgage, food and school transport after both wages shrink.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union to push for a written clinic and factory hours plan, and we'll call the mortgage provider if either rota is cut. If the plant offers a funded, paid-time robot-coating course with a real supervised place and safe isolation practice, I'll enrol. Once qualified, if my factory hours fall, I'll apply to posted local maintenance posts with safe duties and pay and hours that cover our bills; if no place opens, I'll apply for posted local production work at sufficient pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can move quickly, but I expect a major household pay loss before a new skill can protect us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What must robot training teach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to isolate the spray gun, check the oven is cool, then practise stopping the robot arm before a person enters the booth. A demonstration while the conveyor runs would not be safe training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which family costs would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We could cancel the planned school holiday and move the children to free after-school activities if paid hours actually fall. I won't cut the heating while the kids are at home.

say: **2028 thinking AI** could cut clinic calls before robots coat railings around 2031.
The union should demand **income protection** and written hours plans.
think: A large **household wage loss** seems likely with only three weeks saved.
Few **nearby plants** cannot promise a replacement junior wage.
do: **Enrol** in paid robot-coating training if funded supervised place opens.

S2.quote: A demonstration while the conveyor runs would not be safe training.
fieldNote: His **adaptive response** includes paid practical learning, but urgency cannot replace a real course place.
He distinguishes a **qualified maintenance application** from the no-course production fallback, both tied to adequate local pay.

steps.text: Call mortgage provider if either household rota is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If thinking AI reaches clinic bookings in 2031 and capable coating robots arrive around 2034, I'd tell the crew that five years is enough to build a paid route into maintenance. The union still has to secure places, not just course leaflets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the clinic's booking work changes and 51 when physical robots reach my line. We have a mortgage and two children; my current three-week reserve is fragile. If full shifts keep coming, I can learn and add to it before either role changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the paid coating shifts and put a small new amount from every full Saturday into savings after essential bills. If the plant funds a recognized maintenance course with an offered paid-time place, guarded spray-booth practice and a tutor, I'll enrol next term. If qualified and factory hours later fall, I'll apply to posted local maintenance jobs only where regular hours, safe duties and pay meet our costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the real household risk, but five years lets me act without leaving the current wage. The extra time is useful only when the paid shifts arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would practical maintenance learning include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would practise clearing a blocked spray nozzle with the air and powder isolated, then check the finished rail under a lamp. A course without actual booth work would not make me a safe maintenance hire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first savings target?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first target is one month of mortgage, food and school transport. A cancelled coating shift cannot become a savings deposit.

The union should obtain **real paid maintenance places**, not only course leaflets.
think: At **48**, my partner's desk work may shrink while the mortgage remains.
A **one-month reserve** requires full paid Saturdays, not planned shifts.

**Apply** to posted local maintenance roles if qualified, hours fall and pay suffices.

S3.quote: A cancelled coating shift cannot become a savings deposit.
fieldNote: His **new saving** is explicitly conditional on earned Saturday pay.
The **course and application** preserve offered place, funding, safe practical work, qualification and adequate posted wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 may book the clinic patients, and capable robots around 2039 may coat and check rails. I'd tell the union a decade of notice is useful only if training seats and wages appear before cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 when the clinic's booking work changes and 56 when robots can run my physical tasks. Our children will be older, but we will still need a wage and a home. The current three-week reserve and uncertain Saturdays make me worry now, not only in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep learning the existing coating equipment and save a little new money from each full paid month. If the plant offers a funded paid-time maintenance certificate with safe booth practice, I'll take it, then check actual local openings yearly. If either wage falls after 2036, I'll apply for posted local qualified work with safe duties and enough regular pay; I'll keep the current line while it pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our thin margin today, even with ten years to prepare for robots. I can learn quickly, but I can't save wages the factory never pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What record would help test a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep a record of the nozzle checks and the rails rejected for thin coating, so any robot trial can be tested against actual waste. A glossy demonstration would not tell us who pays for rework.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you seek through the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to bargain for paid practice and a written rota notice. If I get a real place, I'll learn the new machine on a closed booth with the safety lead present.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which worries you most, and what would help?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast 2028 case worries me most. The clinic could cut appointment hours before robots reach the coating line around 2031, and we have only three weeks saved. A written hours plan, paid guarded maintenance training and a posted safe local job at enough pay would help us keep the mortgage current.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I should have asked?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the first person offered robot training is the junior operator whose Saturday shifts keep disappearing. A training seat is only a chance if the factory pays us to sit in it.

headlineQuote: A training seat is only a chance if the factory pays us to sit in it.
portrait: **Rafael**, 43, is a junior powder-coating operator with secondary school education and a lower factory wage.
He and his clinic-worker partner support **two schoolchildren** and a mortgage with three weeks of expenses saved.
He uses **AI daily** for fault explanations and wants early access to real safe controls training.
Cancelled Saturdays keep him **anxious** in AI Plateau; expected losses to both wages alarm him in the fast scenario.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could cut his partner’s appointment hours before robots threaten coating-line work around 2031.
